# Overview

The [linear regression vignette](using-rcppensmallen.html) and the
[logistic regression vignette](logistic-regression.html) both hand
[`ensmallen`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html) a class carrying
`Evaluate()` and `Gradient()`. Their objectives are differentiable everywhere,
so the gradient comes in closed form and the optimizer can be chosen for speed.

Least absolute deviations regression removes that choice. Its objective is a
sum of absolute values, and an absolute value has no derivative at zero. A
least absolute deviations fit puts residuals exactly on zero, so the objective
has no gradient at the very point the optimizer is looking for. That settles
which member functions the C++ class can supply, and which optimizers will
accept it.

The C++ below is a fragment of one file, which is included in the package as
`src/example-lad-gradient-free.cpp` and compiled into it as `lad_reg_pso()`.
Because compiling C++ is slow, this vignette displays the source without
rebuilding it and calls the precompiled function to produce the numbers.

# The objective

The design matrix is $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ with entries
$X_{ij}$, the coefficient vector is $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$, and the
response $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is continuous. Indices run
$i = 1, \dots, n$ over observations and $j = 1, \dots, p$ over coefficients. An
intercept is a column of ones inside $\mathbf{X}$ rather than a separate term.

The residual vector collects the $n$ discrepancies between the response and the
fit:

$$r(\beta) = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, \qquad r_i(\beta) = y_i - \sum_{j=1}^{p} X_{ij}\,\beta_j$$

Least squares sums the squares of those residuals. Least absolute deviations
sums their absolute values, collapsing the $n$ of them to one number the same
way:

$$f(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert r_i(\beta) \rvert = \lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\beta \rVert_1 \in \mathbb{R}$$

Doubling a residual doubles its contribution to $f$ and quadruples its
contribution to the residual sum of squares. A response far from the fitted
line therefore pulls a least squares fit toward itself with a force that grows
as it moves away, and pulls a least absolute deviations fit with a force that
does not. That is why $f$ is the fit for data whose errors have heavy tails.

# The missing gradient

The absolute value has derivative $\mathrm{sign}(u)$ for $u \neq 0$ and no
derivative at $u = 0$, where the left and right slopes are $-1$ and $+1$. At a
$\beta$ that leaves every residual away from zero the chain rule applies term by
term, and $\partial r_i / \partial \beta_j = -X_{ij}$ gives

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial \beta_j} = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{ij}\,\mathrm{sign}\left(r_i(\beta)\right), \qquad j = 1, \dots, p$$

$$\nabla f(\beta) = -\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathrm{sign}\left(r(\beta)\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$$

A least absolute deviations fit for a design with $p$ columns passes exactly
through $p$ of the observations, so $p$ residuals are zero and the expression
above is undefined at the answer it is meant to find. The
[verification](#verifying-the-result) below counts those residuals, and the
second panel of the figure shows the kink they produce.

Away from the solution the formula is no better behaved. $\mathrm{sign}$
reports plus or minus one however small a residual gets, so the vector it
returns never shrinks as the fit improves, and a gradient method reads a
vanishing gradient as convergence. The class therefore supplies the objective
and stops.

# The arbitrary function contract

`ensmallen` sorts objectives by which member functions they define, and each
optimizer states which of those sets it can work with. A class carrying
`Evaluate()` alone is an
[arbitrary function](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#arbitrary-functions).

| Contract | Member functions |
|---|---|
| Arbitrary | `Evaluate()` |
| Differentiable | `Evaluate()`, `Gradient()` |
| Differentiable separable | `Evaluate()` and `Gradient()` over a batch, `NumFunctions()`, `Shuffle()` |
| Constrained | `Evaluate()`, `Gradient()`, `NumConstraints()`, `EvaluateConstraint()`, `GradientConstraint()` |

Reading down the table, the contracts get more demanding and the set of
optimizers that accept them gets smaller. This vignette sits on the first row;
the [logistic regression vignette](logistic-regression.html) writes the second
and third, and the [constrained optimization
vignette](constrained-optimization.html) the fourth.

Every standalone file using `RcppEnsmallen` opens with the same two lines, the
attribute telling `Rcpp::sourceCpp()` where to find the headers.

```{Rcpp header, eval = FALSE}
#include <RcppEnsmallen.h>
// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppEnsmallen)]]
```

The class holds the data and computes one number from a coefficient vector.

```{Rcpp classdef, eval = FALSE}
// Define an arbitrary objective function by implementing Evaluate() and
// nothing else.
class LADFunction
{
public:
    // Construct the object with the given design matrix and responses.
    LADFunction(const arma::mat& X,
                const arma::vec& y) :
    X(X), y(y) { }

    // Return the objective function for model parameters beta.
    double Evaluate(const arma::mat& beta)
    {
        return arma::accu(arma::abs(y - X * beta));
    }

private:
    // The design matrix.
    const arma::mat& X;
    // The responses to each data point.
    const arma::vec& y;
};
```

`y - X * beta` is the $n \times 1$ residual vector, and `arma::abs()` acts on
it elementwise. `arma::accu()` sums the result to the one number `Evaluate()`
returns. `beta` arrives as a $p \times 1$ matrix, one entry per column of `X`,
as it does in the differentiable classes.

# A contract mismatch

The pairing between a class and an optimizer is checked when the file is
compiled, not when it runs. Substituting
[`ens::CMAES<>`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#cma-es) for the optimizer
used below and rebuilding gives three errors, of which these two carry the
information. Paths, line numbers and instantiation traces are cut, and long
lines wrapped:

```
error: no member named 'NumFunctions' in 'LADFunction'
   const size_t numFunctions = function.NumFunctions();

error: static assertion failed due to requirement
'CheckSeparableEvaluate<LADFunction, arma::Mat<double>,
arma::Mat<double>>::value': The FunctionType does not have a correct
definition of Evaluate(). Please check that the FunctionType fully satisfies
the requirements of the ArbitrarySeparableFunctionType API; see the optimizer
tutorial for more details.
```

The second message names the contract CMA-ES wants, the arbitrary *separable*
one, which asks for `Evaluate()` over a batch of data points and a
`NumFunctions()` reporting how many there are. That is a different row of the
table above, and the first message names the missing member function outright.

The static checks live in
`inst/include/ensmallen_bits/function/static_checks.hpp`, where each contract
carries a message naming itself, so a build failure identifies the API the
optimizer expects without looking the optimizer up first.

# Running the optimizer

[`ens::LBestPSO`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#pso) is a local best
particle swarm optimizer. It scatters candidate coefficient vectors across the
search space and moves each one toward the best point it has seen and the best
point its neighbors have seen, using nothing but the objective values it
collects along the way.

```{Rcpp ladpso, eval = FALSE}
// [[Rcpp::export]]
arma::vec lad_reg_pso(const arma::mat& X, const arma::vec& y) {

    // Construct the objective function.
    LADFunction ladf(X, y);

    // Create the local best particle swarm optimizer with default parameters.
    // The ens::LBestPSO type can be replaced with any ensmallen optimizer that
    // can handle arbitrary functions, meaning ones that supply Evaluate()
    // alone.
    ens::LBestPSO pso;

    // Create a starting point for our optimization. The swarm is placed at
    // random, so only the shape of this matrix is read. The model has p
    // parameters, so the shape is p x 1.
    arma::mat beta(X.n_cols, 1, arma::fill::zeros);

    // Run the optimization. The swarm draws through R's random number
    // generator, so set.seed() on the R side pins the result.
    pso.Optimize(ladf, beta);

    return beta;
}
```

The zeros are read for their dimensions and then overwritten, a departure from
the L-BFGS examples where the starting values are the point the search begins
at.

The included file adds a block of `Rcpp::stop()` argument checks at the top of
this function, omitted here so the optimizer setup stays in view. They reject a
non-finite `X` or `y`, since a single `NA` makes the objective non-finite for
every particle, leaving the swarm nothing to move toward and returning the
untouched starting point as if it were a fit. The response is continuous, so
the check on `y` is finiteness rather than the membership in $\{0, 1\}$ the
logistic examples require.

**Note:** the `// [[Rcpp::export]]` attribute has to appear in the `.cpp` file
Rcpp compiles, but the class does not have to. Moving the class into a header
beside it and including it with `#include` works under both `sourceCpp()` and a
package build.

# Verifying the result

The simulation draws its errors from a $t$ distribution with two degrees of
freedom, which has no finite variance, since heavy tails are the setting this
loss is for.

```{r data-generation}
n <- 400
beta <- c(2, -1.5, 0.8)
p <- length(beta)

set.seed(512)

# Design matrix with an intercept column
X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(n * (p - 1)), ncol = p - 1))

# Continuous responses with heavy tailed errors
y <- as.vector(X %*% beta + rt(n, df = 2))
```

`optim(method = "Nelder-Mead")` is the base R comparison. Like the particle
swarm it never asks for a derivative, so both solvers work from the same
information about the same surface.

```{r estimation}
obj <- function(b) sum(abs(y - X %*% b))

set.seed(512)
fit <- lad_reg_pso(X, y)

nm <- optim(rep(0, p), obj, method = "Nelder-Mead",
            control = list(maxit = 20000, reltol = 1e-12))
```

```{r comparison-table, echo = FALSE}
compare_coefs <- cbind(beta, as.vector(fit), nm$par)
colnames(compare_coefs) <- c("Truth", "LBestPSO", "Nelder-Mead")
rownames(compare_coefs) <- paste0("Beta", seq_len(nrow(compare_coefs)))
knitr::kable(compare_coefs, digits = 6, longtable = FALSE,
             caption = "Comparison of Estimated Coefficients")
```

The two solvers agree to three decimal places, and each sits further from the
truth than from the other. The gap to the generating parameters is sampling
error at $n = 400$ with $t_2$ noise, not optimizer error.

```{r agreement}
max(abs(as.vector(fit) - nm$par))
```

Coefficients are the loose measure here. A piecewise linear surface is flat
along the directions that move a coefficient without moving any residual across
zero, so two solvers can stop at visibly different points of the same flat
region. The objective is the tight measure, and the one being minimized:

```{r objective}
c(LBestPSO = obj(fit), NelderMead = nm$value)

obj(fit) - nm$value
```

The swarm reaches the lower value of the two. Nelder-Mead closes the remaining
gap when it is restarted from its own answer until it stops improving, which is
the reference the package tests measure against; a single call from a vector of
zeros stops short.

The $p$ zero residuals asserted earlier are visible in the fit:

```{r residuals}
resid <- as.vector(y - X %*% fit)
sort(abs(resid))[1:5]
```

The three smallest, one per column of `X`, fall below 1e-9, and the fourth is
larger than the third by seven orders of magnitude. The fitted plane passes
through three of the four hundred points exactly, and the objective has no
derivative there.

The formula a `Gradient()` would have used has length of order one at the fit
rather than of order zero, and stepping a millionth of a unit away does not
shrink it.

```{r nonvanishing}
grad <- function(b) -as.vector(t(X) %*% sign(as.vector(y - X %*% b)))

set.seed(9)
step <- rnorm(p)
step <- step / sqrt(sum(step^2))

c(at_the_fit = sqrt(sum(grad(fit)^2)),
  a_step_away = sqrt(sum(grad(fit + 1e-6 * step)^2)))
```

An optimizer watching that number for a signal to stop would wait forever.

Holding the first and third coefficients at their fitted values and varying the
second gives a one-dimensional slice of the objective. It is drawn twice below,
once over a wide window beside the squared-error loss on the same data, and
once magnified around the minimum.

```{r kink-plot, fig.width = 6.8, fig.height = 3.4, parset = list(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.1, 4.3, 3.1, 1.1)), fig.alt = "Two panels. The left panel plots the absolute and squared error objectives against the second coefficient over a window three units wide, both rescaled to a common range; the two curves are bowl shaped and nearly indistinguishable near the bottom. The right panel magnifies the absolute error objective around its minimum, where it is a chain of straight segments joined at marked breakpoints, with a sharp corner at the minimum rather than a smooth turn."}
hold <- X[, 1] * fit[1] + X[, 3] * fit[3]
l1 <- function(b2) sum(abs(y - hold - X[, 2] * b2))
sse <- function(b2) sum((y - hold - X[, 2] * b2)^2)

# Left: both losses over a wide window, each shifted to its own minimum and
# scaled to a common range so they share an axis.
wide <- seq(fit[2] - 1.5, fit[2] + 1.5, length.out = 400)
rescale <- function(v) (v - min(v)) / diff(range(v))
plot(wide, rescale(vapply(wide, l1, 0)), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#1b6ca8",
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = expression(beta[2]),
     ylab = "Objective, rescaled", main = "Both losses")
lines(wide, rescale(vapply(wide, sse, 0)), lwd = 2, col = "#c0392b", lty = 2)
legend("top", bty = "n", cex = 0.8, legend = c("Absolute", "Squared"),
       col = c("#1b6ca8", "#c0392b"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2)

# Right: the absolute loss near the minimum. A kink sits at every b2 that
# sends one residual through zero.
kinks <- (y - hold) / X[, 2]
halfw <- sort(abs(kinks - fit[2]))[8]
near <- kinks[abs(kinks - fit[2]) <= halfw]
zoom <- seq(fit[2] - halfw, fit[2] + halfw, length.out = 1500)
plot(zoom, vapply(zoom, l1, 0), type = "n", xlab = expression(beta[2]),
     ylab = "Sum of absolute residuals", main = "Absolute, magnified")
abline(v = near, col = "grey80", lty = 3)
lines(zoom, vapply(zoom, l1, 0), lwd = 2, col = "#1b6ca8")
points(near, vapply(near, l1, 0), pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = "#1b6ca8")
points(fit[2], l1(fit[2]), pch = 4, cex = 1.7, lwd = 2, col = "#c0392b")
```

At the scale of the left panel both curves look like smooth bowls that a
gradient method could descend. The right panel covers a window a few percent as
wide. There the absolute loss is a chain of straight segments whose slope
changes at each dotted line. Each dotted line is a value of $\beta_2$ that sends
one residual through zero. The minimum, marked with a cross, is a corner
rather than a smooth turn, the slope arriving negative and leaving positive
with nothing in between. Each break changes the slope by
$2\lvert X_{i2} \rvert$, which is why the breaks belonging to small entries of
the second column are hard to see.

# Choosing an optimizer

Five optimizers in `ensmallen` accept a class shaped like `LADFunction`.
Swapping the type on one line of `lad_reg_pso()` is the whole change:

```{Rcpp swap, eval = FALSE}
    ens::LBestPSO pso;   // ens::SA<>, ens::CNE, ens::SPSA and ens::DE also
                         // accept a class that supplies Evaluate() alone.
```

Run at their default settings on the data generated above, each seeded with
`set.seed(512)` and started from a vector of zeros, they separate clearly. The
reference is Nelder-Mead restarted from its own answer until it stops
improving, which reaches 657.916218 on this data, and the gap column reports
how far above that each optimizer stopped.

| Optimizer | Objective | Gap to the reference |
|---|---|---|
| `ens::LBestPSO` | 657.916218 | 1.9e-10 |
| `ens::SA<>` | 657.916432 | 2.1e-04 |
| `ens::CNE` | 657.949083 | 3.3e-02 |
| `ens::SPSA` | 658.023219 | 1.1e-01 |
| `ens::DE` | 662.798752 | 4.9e+00 |

The swarm matches the reference to 2e-10 on the objective and to 3.5e-10 on the
worst coefficient, which is why `lad_reg_pso()` uses it. Simulated annealing
lands close behind. Conventional neural evolution and simultaneous perturbation
stochastic approximation stop at points that are visibly worse but still
recognizable as the fit.

Differential evolution at its defaults misses badly, by roughly five units of
objective and 0.23 in the worst coefficient. Its own header says as much. The
constructor takes a population size, a maximum number of generations, a
crossover rate and a differential weight. The comment above it warns that "the
default values provided over here are not necessarily suitable for a given
function" and recommends adjusting them to the problem.

Nothing in the vector it returns announces the failure. The coefficients have
the right signs and roughly the right magnitudes, and a gradient-free optimizer
leaves behind no gradient to test for flatness where it stopped. The table
catches it by running a second solver on the same data and comparing
objectives.

These numbers are one run on one data set. Hold the data, the seed and the
starting point fixed, change one type, and compare the objective rather than
the coefficients.

# The specialist solver

Nelder-Mead is another general purpose search. The check below is against the
solver built for this problem. Least absolute deviations is median regression,
the $\tau = 0.5$ case of quantile regression, and `quantreg::rq()` is the
established R implementation. It does not search at all. It writes the fit as a
linear program and solves that exactly. The swarm walks toward the corner of
the objective; `rq` computes which corner it is.

```{r quantreg-fit, eval = requireNamespace("quantreg", quietly = TRUE)}
rq_beta <- as.vector(coef(quantreg::rq(y ~ X - 1, tau = 0.5)))

c(LBestPSO = obj(fit), rq = obj(rq_beta))

obj(fit) - obj(rq_beta)

max(abs(as.vector(fit) - rq_beta))
```

Both reach an objective of 657.916218. The swarm sits 1.9e-10 above the exact
solution, and the two coefficient vectors differ by at most 3.5e-10. On this
data the swarm found the right point.

Agreement is half a benchmark. The other half is what each answer cost. The
swarm is timed with its seed reset every repetition, so each measured call does
the same work as the one in the fit above.

```{r quantreg-timing, eval = requireNamespace("quantreg", quietly = TRUE)}
pso_reps <- 10
rq_reps <- 200

pso_time <- system.time(
  for (i in seq_len(pso_reps)) {
    set.seed(512)
    lad_reg_pso(X, y)
  }
)[["elapsed"]] / pso_reps

rq_time <- system.time(
  for (i in seq_len(rq_reps)) quantreg::rq(y ~ X - 1, tau = 0.5)
)[["elapsed"]] / rq_reps

c(LBestPSO = pso_time, rq = rq_time)

pso_time / rq_time
```

The ratio ran into the hundreds on every run measured here. `ens::LBestPSO`
defaults to 64 particles and up to 3000 iterations, and evaluates the objective
once per particle per iteration. A simplex method on a linear program of this
size does far less arithmetic.

A general purpose optimizer reached the answer a specialist solver reaches, and
paid two orders of magnitude in time to get there. When a specialist solver
exists for your objective, use the specialist. `ensmallen` earns its place on
the objectives that have no specialist, or the ones you wrote yourself and
nobody has solved before. `LADFunction` is twenty lines and required no
knowledge of linear programming.

# Seeding

The swarm is drawn through Armadillo's random number generator, which
`RcppArmadillo` routes onto R's own stream, so a fixed seed makes a run
reproducible exactly as it does for the mini-batch optimizer in the logistic
regression vignette:

```{r seeding}
set.seed(20260818); first  <- lad_reg_pso(X, y)
set.seed(20260818); second <- lad_reg_pso(X, y)
identical(first, second)
```

The same mechanism means a call consumes random numbers from R's stream and
shifts whatever draws follow it. Unseeded runs land at slightly different
points on the surface, and the spread widens as `X` gains columns, so seed
every call whose result is compared against a fixed number.

# The included file

`src/example-lad-gradient-free.cpp` holds the class, the exported function, the
argument checks omitted above, and the roxygen block behind `?lad_reg_pso`. The
[logistic regression
vignette](logistic-regression.html#moving-this-into-an-r-package) covers moving
a standalone file into a package.

The [constrained optimization vignette](constrained-optimization.html) takes
the last row of the contract table, where the class supplies `Evaluate()` and
`Gradient()` and three more member functions besides.
